subject: general
question: What is the approximate time period of second phase of the green revolution in India?
solution:
The correct answer is __**mid- 1970s to mid-1980s**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Green Revolution** in India was a period when Indian agriculture was converted into an industrial system due to the adoption of modern methods and technology. It is generally categorized into **two distinct phases**.
 
• The **second phase** of the Green Revolution approximately spanned from the **mid-1970s to the mid-1980s**. ***Hence, the correct answer is mid- 1970s to mid-1980s.***
 
• During this **second phase**, the **High-Yielding Variety (HYV) technology** spread to a much larger number of states and benefited a more diverse range of crops beyond just wheat and rice.
 
• While the **first phase** (mid-1960s to mid-1970s) was restricted to affluent states like **Punjab**, **Haryana**, and **Western Uttar Pradesh**, the **second phase** saw expansion into states like **Andhra Pradesh**, **Tamil Nadu**, and parts of the **Eastern region**.
 
• This geographical spread was crucial in ensuring that the benefits of increased **food grain production** were distributed more equitably across the country, helping India move closer to total **food self-sufficiency**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Origins of Green Revolution:**

 
 
• The revolution was initiated in the **1960s** by introducing **Mexican wheat varieties**.
 
• **M.S. Swaminathan** is known as the **Father of the Green Revolution in India** for his leadership and role in introducing and further developing **HYV** wheat varieties.
 
• Globally, **Norman Borlaug** is hailed as the **Father of the Green Revolution** and was awarded the **Nobel Peace Prize** in **1970** for his work.
 
 
 
• **Core Components:**
 
 
• **HYV Seeds:** These seeds had a higher yield potential compared to traditional seeds but required a reliable supply of **water** and the correct proportion of **fertilizers** and **pesticides**.
 
• **Irrigation:** The success of the revolution was heavily dependent on **assured irrigation facilities**, leading to the construction of various **dams** and **tube wells**.
 
• **Chemical Inputs:** Increased use of **chemical fertilizers**, **pesticides**, and **weedicides** was necessary to protect and nourish the high-yielding crops.
 
 
 
• **Economic Impact:**
 
 
• It resulted in a significant increase in the **productivity** of food grains, especially **wheat** and **rice**.
 
• The surplus production allowed the government to maintain a **buffer stock** through the **Food Corporation of India (FCI)**, which could be used during times of food shortage.
 
• It enabled the **commercialization of agriculture** as farmers began producing for the market rather than just for **subsistence**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Phases Comparison:**

 
 
• **Phase I (mid-1960s to mid-1970s):** Characterized by the use of **HYV seeds** primarily in wheat-growing regions like **Punjab** and **Haryana**.
 
• **Phase II (mid-1970s to mid-1980s):** Marked by the spread of technology to other states and inclusion of **rice** and other crops in the **HYV** net.
 
 
 
• **Government Policy:**
 
 
• The government provided **loans at low-interest rates** and **subsidized fertilizers** so that small farmers could also afford the necessary inputs.
 
• This intervention was vital to prevent the "rich getting richer" syndrome and to make the **Green Revolution** inclusive for small-scale landholders.
 
 
 
• **Environmental Concerns:** While the revolution solved **hunger**, it later faced criticism for **soil degradation**, **depletion of groundwater**, and the loss of **biodiversity** due to **monocropping**.
